_note: Content seed for the Practice engine. Each item is a spoken-rehearsal drill: prompt = what to say out loud; reference = read-only 'what good looks like' to reveal AFTER an attempt. The user's own answer + all progress fields (confidence, nextPracticeAt, etc.) are user-owned and must never be overwritten by the loader. Wrap/track-assign to match interview.json.

items.prompt: Scenario: a deal review on a $2M BFSI renewal has drifted into status updates and nobody is deciding anything. Out loud, intervene using OOR. State what you observe, the two real options, and your recommendation. Say it three times — slower the second time, lower-toned the third. Land on the recommendation, pause two seconds, and stop. No trailing words.

reference.framework: OOR — Observation → Option → Recommendation. Use for a decisive, structured intervention.
reference.pattern: I'm observing X. Options are A or B. I recommend Y, because Z.
reference.model: I'm observing we're three weeks from renewal with no executive sponsor engaged. Two options: we keep working the champion and hope it lands, or we escalate now and ask their COO for 20 minutes. I recommend we escalate this week — the cost of delay is a slipped quarter, and we still have the relationship to do it cleanly.
reference.watchOut: Don't pre-justify before anyone challenges you. State the recommendation once and stop — over-explaining signals the position is weak.
reference.delivery: Recommendation → 2-second pause → silence. End on a verb or noun, not a filler.

items.prompt: Scenario: a forecast call has gone tactical — everyone is debating which feature demo to run next. Out loud, reframe to the business level using FBT: name the frame, the business impact, and the trade-off. Repeat three times, removing 20% of the words each pass until it is one tight breath.

reference.framework: FBT — Frame → Business impact → Trade-off. Use when the conversation drifts tactical.
reference.pattern: At the business level: X. Impact: Y. Trade-off: Z.
reference.model: At the business level, this account is deciding whether we're a vendor or a platform. Impact: the platform path is three times the ACV but needs their CIO bought in. The trade-off is speed — we can close small this quarter, or play for the bigger mandate next.
reference.watchOut: Don't rescue the group with tactical detail — that keeps you in executor mode. Stay at the business level.
reference.delivery: Lead with the frame, not the background. Max 12–15 words per sentence.

items.prompt: Scenario: a QBR is drowning in dashboards and pipeline metrics. Out loud, cut through it with the SO WHAT? move — convert one data point into a decision-relevant meaning in two sentences. Then say it again, even shorter.

reference.framework: SO WHAT? — Meaning extraction. Use in data-heavy discussions.
reference.pattern: So what changes for us? → [the implication], → [the decision it forces].
reference.model: Win rates on net-new are flat but expansion is up 40%. So what — our motion is shifting from hunting to farming. The implication: we should be reallocating two reps from new-logo to the install base now, not next half.
reference.watchOut: Don't recite the data back. The room already saw the chart — your value is the meaning, not the number.
reference.delivery: Headline the implication first (BLUF), then the one supporting fact.

items.prompt: Scenario: leadership is fuzzy on whether to pursue a high-risk transformation deal with a long sales cycle. Out loud, bring rigor with D.A.R.E: state the decision, the assumptions it rests on, the risks, and the exit criteria. Deliver it as if briefing your VP in under 40 seconds.

reference.framework: D.A.R.E — Decision → Assumptions → Risks → Exit criteria. Use when ambiguity or risk tolerance is fuzzy.
reference.pattern: The decision is X. We're assuming Y. The risks are Z. Our exit criteria are W.
reference.model: The decision is to commit a solution engineer to this transformation deal for one quarter. We're assuming their CIO mandate is real and funded. The risk is a 12-month cycle with no near-term revenue. Exit criteria: if we don't have economic-buyer access by week six, we step back to a lighter engagement.
reference.watchOut: Naming exit criteria is a strength, not weakness — it shows judgment, not doubt. Say it cleanly.
reference.delivery: Four crisp beats, one breath each. Pause before 'exit criteria' — that's the executive move.

items.prompt: Scenario: your manager asks what your team should focus on next half across five competing priorities. Out loud, answer with N/S/E — Now, Soon, Eventually — naming one thing in each. Say it three times until the sequencing sounds inevitable, not improvised.

reference.framework: N/S/E — Now → Soon → Eventually. Use when prioritization and sequencing are needed.
reference.pattern: Now: X. Soon: Y. Eventually: Z.
reference.model: Now, we lock the two renewals at risk — that's revenue we already counted. Soon, we build the BFSI reference story so the next three deals move faster. Eventually, we expand into insurance, but only once the banking motion is repeatable.
keyPhrases: if we do only one thing
reference.watchOut: Don't list all five priorities — that's flooding. Force the choice: one per horizon.
reference.delivery: Three beats, descending tone. The 'Now' should sound non-negotiable.

items.prompt: Scenario: the team jumps straight to building a custom POC before agreeing what they're solving. Out loud, anchor the conversation with POC — Problem, Outcome we want, Constraints. Repeat twice; the second time, lead with an even sharper one-line problem statement.

reference.framework: POC — Problem → Outcome → Constraints. Use when people jump to solutions.
reference.pattern: Let's anchor: the problem is X, the outcome we want is Y, the constraints are Z.
reference.model: Let's anchor before we build. The problem is the customer can't prove ROI to their board. The outcome we want is a number they'll defend internally. The constraint is we have two weeks and no access to their finance team — so the POC has to generate that proof itself.
reference.watchOut: Solving before framing is a presence-killer. Resist the urge to propose the solution until the problem is agreed.
reference.delivery: Calm volume. You're slowing the room down on purpose — that itself signals control.

items.prompt: Scenario: your VP catches you in the hallway and asks 'how's the Santander account?' You have ten seconds. Out loud, answer with S3 — Situation, Signal, Significance — no long context. Say it three times, each one tighter.

reference.framework: S3 — Situation → Signal → Significance. Use when you want to sound sharp without long context.
reference.pattern: Situation: X. The signal is Y. That matters because Z.
reference.model: Situation: we're in final procurement. The signal is their CFO joined the last call unprompted. That matters because it means budget is no longer the blocker — legal is now the only thing between us and signature.
reference.watchOut: Don't open with three minutes of history. Situation in one line, then straight to the signal.
reference.delivery: Downward inflection on 'signature.' Finish the thought — don't trail up like a question.

items.prompt: Scenario: you have 30 seconds in a packed leadership meeting to update on a strategic account. Out loud, use BCF — Bottom line, Context, Follow-up. Deliver it, pause, stop. Then re-run it 10 seconds shorter.

reference.framework: BCF — Bottom line → Context → Follow-up. Use when time is short and you want authority.
reference.pattern: Bottom line: X. Context: Y. Next step: Z.
reference.model: Bottom line: the AXA deal will close this quarter, but smaller than forecast. Context: they cut scope to one business unit to hit their own budget freeze. Next step: I'm setting up the expansion conversation for Q2 with their group CIO.
reference.watchOut: Don't bury the lead. If the room only hears your first sentence, it should still be the most important thing.
reference.delivery: Bottom line in under 15 words. Pause after the next step — resist adding a fourth point.

items.prompt: Scenario: you see a real delivery risk on a flagship account, but you don't want to be 'the blocker' in front of leadership. Out loud, raise it with RGR — Risk, Guardrail, Recommendation. Say it twice, the second time warmer in tone but just as firm.

reference.framework: RGR — Risk → Guardrail → Recommendation. Use when raising risk without being the blocker.
reference.pattern: The risk is X. The guardrail is Y. My recommendation is Z.
reference.model: The risk is we're promising a go-live date that depends on their data migration, which they own and haven't started. The guardrail is a joint milestone plan with their IT lead by Friday. My recommendation: we commit to the date contingent on that plan, not before.
reference.watchOut: Don't just name the risk and stop — that's what 'the blocker' does. Always carry a guardrail and a recommendation.
reference.delivery: Calm, even tone throughout. You're solving, not warning.

items.prompt: Scenario: a senior leader proposes discounting deeply to win a logo, and you disagree. Out loud, push back with DDI — Disagree, Data, Invite — keeping your status and your calm. Repeat three times; on the third, say it as if the room is skeptical of you.

reference.framework: DDI — Disagree → Data → Invite. Use when you disagree and want to keep status and calm.
reference.pattern: I see it differently. Here's the data/logic. I'm open to pressure-testing.
reference.model: I see this differently. The last three deals we discounted to win never expanded — they anchored low and stayed low. My read is we hold price and trade on payment terms instead. Happy to pressure-test that if I'm missing something.
reference.watchOut: No hedging ('maybe I'm wrong, but…') and no apology for disagreeing. State your view as a view, with data, calmly.
reference.delivery: Open with 'I see it differently' — full stop, slight pause. Conviction without volume.

items.prompt: Scenario: you need a senior exec to make a customer call to unblock a stalled deal, and you don't want to sound needy. Out loud, ask with C-A-R — Context, Ask, Rationale. Say it twice; the second time, make the ask a single clean sentence.

reference.framework: C-A-R — Context → Ask → Rationale. Use when you need help/a decision/an escalation without sounding needy.
reference.pattern: Context: X. My ask is Y. Rationale: Z.
reference.model: Context: we're at the final stage on a £3M deal and their CEO wants peer-level reassurance before signing. My ask is 20 minutes of your time for a CEO-to-CEO call this week. Rationale: it's the one thing standing between us and signature, and it's a relationship only you can open.
reference.watchOut: Status leakage kills this — no 'sorry to bother you,' no 'if you have time maybe.' Make the ask directly; the rationale earns it.
reference.delivery: The ask is one sentence, stated plainly. Don't shrink your voice on it.

items.prompt: Scenario: a cross-functional debate is stuck arguing about which integration to build first. Out loud, raise the altitude with the 'one level up' move — reframe what the debate is actually about. Repeat twice until the reframe feels obvious.

reference.framework: One level up — Decision-lens escalation. Use when a debate is stuck at the wrong altitude.
reference.pattern: One level up, this is really about X.
reference.model: One level up, this isn't about which integration ships first — it's about whether we're building for this one account or for a repeatable BFSI platform. If it's the platform, the sequencing answers itself.
reference.watchOut: Don't win the small argument — dissolve it by moving up a level. That's what makes the room look to you.
reference.delivery: Slow down on 'one level up.' Let the reframe land before you continue.

items.prompt: Scenario: leadership is excited about a big multi-year bet and nobody is naming risk. Out loud, introduce executive risk-thinking with a pre-mortem — 'assume this failed in six months, what caused it?' Then answer your own question in two crisp causes. Say it twice.

reference.framework: PRE-MORTEM — 'Assume it failed.' Use when you want executive risk-thinking in the room.
reference.pattern: Assume this fails in six months — what caused it? → [cause 1], [cause 2].
reference.model: Let's assume this fails in six months. Two likely causes: we never got a single-threaded owner on their side, so it died in committee — or we underestimated the data migration and lost trust on the first milestone. If those are the failure modes, let's design against them now.
reference.watchOut: Frame it as rigor, not pessimism. You're the person making the bet safer, not the one doubting it.
reference.delivery: Ask the question, pause, let it sit. The pause is the presence.

items.prompt: Scenario: a meeting is winding down with lots of agreement but no clear ownership. Out loud, close it with WHO/WHAT/WHEN — convert the talk into action in one sentence per item, without sounding tactical. Re-run it once, crisper.

reference.framework: WHO/WHAT/WHEN — Crisp execution close. Use to turn talk into action without sounding tactical.
reference.pattern: Who owns it, what exactly is delivered, by when?
reference.model: Before we close: I'll own the executive escalation, the deliverable is a signed mutual action plan, and I'll have it back to this group by next Thursday. Anything I'm missing?
reference.watchOut: Don't let a good meeting end without ownership — that's where presence and follow-through get noticed. Close it.
reference.delivery: Confident, brisk, decisive. End on the date, then stop.

items.prompt: Storytelling drill. Pick one real win from your career. Out loud, tell it in this shape: Situation → tension → the action YOU drove → business outcome. Then tell the same story in 60 seconds. Then 30. Then a 15-second headline version. Each pass: stronger opening, clearer ownership, more business significance.

reference.framework: Executive story arc: Situation → Tension → Your action → Business outcome → Why it mattered.
reference.pattern: Open with stakes. Make the tension visible. Own the action ('I drove…'). Land the business result with a number.
reference.model: A top-10 bank was about to churn after a failed rollout. I personally rebuilt the executive relationship, restructured the deployment into 30-day value milestones, and got their COO to sponsor it. We saved a $1.8M renewal and expanded it 40% the next year. It mattered because it became our reference for every bank deal since.
reference.watchOut: Reject the flat version — too much description, passive voice, no stakes, no number. The story must show YOUR judgment and a business outcome.
reference.delivery: The 15-second headline is the real test: stakes + your action + result, in one breath.

items.prompt: Pressure-recovery drill. Have someone (or imagine someone) cut in mid-answer with 'Can you get to the point?' Out loud, recover cleanly: stop, breathe, give the headline in one sentence, then one supporting line. Run this three times with three different topics — the goal is to make recovery automatic.

reference.framework: Recovery sequence: Stop → breathe → headline first → one supporting sentence → stop.
reference.pattern: The short version is X. The reason it matters is Y.
reference.model: Fair — the short version is we'll close this quarter but smaller than planned. The reason it matters is the expansion path is intact, so the number recovers next quarter.
reference.watchOut: Don't apologize or speed up when challenged — that's status leakage. Slow down, reset, lead with the conclusion.
reference.delivery: A two-second pause before the headline reads as control, not as being caught out.

items.prompt: Delivery drill — BLUF + hedge removal. Take any update you'd normally give and say it twice. First pass: lead with the conclusion (Bottom Line Up Front), support after. Second pass: strip every hedge — replace 'maybe / kind of / I think' with 'my view is / the implication is.' Notice how much shorter and more senior it sounds.

reference.framework: Two delivery rules combined: (1) Lead with the headline (BLUF). (2) Remove hedges.
reference.pattern: Conclusion first → support. And: 'my view is…' not 'I think maybe…'.
reference.model: Weak: 'I think maybe we should kind of consider escalating, because it seems like things might be slipping.' Strong: 'My view is we escalate this week. The deal is slipping and we still have the relationship to do it cleanly.'
reference.watchOut: Hedging and over-context are the two fastest presence-killers. Cut both ruthlessly.
reference.delivery: Calm volume, downward inflection, period energy. End sentences like you mean them.

items.prompt: Executive-questions drill. Instead of making a statement to look smart, practice elevating the room with a question. Out loud, deliver three of these to an imaginary stalled meeting, calmly and slowly: 'What problem are we actually solving?' / 'What would make this a bad decision in six months?' / 'If we don't do this, what breaks?' Say each one, pause, and let it hang.

reference.framework: Elevate with questions, not just statements. A sharp question often moves the room faster than a point.
reference.pattern: Ask the directional question → pause → let the room reorient.
reference.model: Before we go further — what problem are we actually solving here? Because if it's the CFO's board narrative, we're building the wrong thing.
keyPhrases: what are we implicitly betting on
reference.watchOut: Silently check yourself first: is my contribution directional, decisional, or just decorative? If decorative, ask a question instead.
reference.delivery: Ask slowly. The pause after the question is where the authority lives — don't fill it.
